seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 2: Declared, Not Signed
blurb: Petra refuses the clerk's wording, and the Bank gives her until midnight to sign a lie.

blocks.text: I wrote '47, surplus, warm' on the variance line of the Close declaration and turned the form round to face the clerk.

He read it twice. His pen came down and stopped above the word 'warm'. Then he drew one straight line through it, and beside it, in a neater hand than the one he kept his ledger in, he wrote 'calibration error'.
'Sign here, Miss Sandor,' he said, 'and your draw stands.'
He turned the paper round to face me and held out the pen.

I looked at his hand, not the pen. Ink on the second finger. A bitten nail on the thumb. The hand was quite steady. My verdict was that he had written those two words before, on other forms, and did not think of them as a lie.
'I checked the empty pan before I weighed,' I said. 'It read nothing. Then it read a hundred and twenty-four. The jar should hold seventy-seven. That isn't a calibration error.'
'The Bank rules on a surplus, Miss Sandor. Not the Reckoner.'
'Then let the Bank rule on what I weighed.'
'It will rule within seven days whatever you sign,' he said. 'This only saves it the trouble.'
'I'll sign my figures. I won't sign yours.'

He did not argue. He wrote the time in his ledger, twelve minutes past twelve, and beside it, 'Declared, not signed.' He lifted the jar into a canvas bag with the Bank's seal on the flap and tied the neck. Then he looked at the Stall Book page, which was still blank.
'Nothing in the Stall Book?'
'No.'
'Then it all comes when it likes,' he said, and closed the ledger.

I copied the figures into my own notebook before I left the lodge: Issue three hundred, spent two hundred and twenty-three, banked seventy-seven, weighed a hundred and twenty-four, forty-seven over. The Bank had my declaration. I wanted my own copy of it.
Whitlow was sitting on the bottom step of the Ninth Stair with his hat on his knee. I gave him back his key. He turned it over once in his palm and put it in his waistcoat pocket.
'Did you sign?' he asked.
'No.'
He did not ask what I had refused to sign, and I did not tell him. He yawned, and covered it with the hat, and looked at me over the brim as if he had not.
'The Bank can't take a licence back,' he said, 'once it has given one.'
'I know. I read it at your table. It hasn't given me one yet.'
'No,' he said. 'It hasn't. And what would you do, Miss Sandor, if you were the Bank, with a Reckoner who won't sign?'
I did not have an answer for him. He stood up slowly, one hand on the rail, and walked me as far as the Guild gate without saying anything else.

The Week of Grace began that morning. I knew the rule. With nothing written in a Stall Book, every second the Ninth Stair had spent would come back as stalls in chunks of one to ten minutes, at moments of their own choosing, waking or asleep, inside seven days. I had read it in print. I had not seen it.
I saw it on the second evening, in the chophouse by the Ninth Stair's gate. Lisle had told me the Reckoner ate with the side the week after a match.
'Custom,' she said. 'Reckoner pays the first round.'
It was not in the printed Laws, so I asked Tran if it was true. Tran said 'mm'. I paid the first round.

Lisle sat with her back to the wall so she could see the room. Drewe sat beside her with a screwdriver in her fingers, turning it end over end on the tablecloth. Tran sat across from me with his eyes half shut and his hands round a cup he did not drink from.
A waiter came out of the kitchen with four plates along one arm.
'Two coppers says he drops one before the corner,' Lisle said.
'Done,' said Drewe.
He dropped one before the corner. It broke on the tiles, and the room turned to look. Lisle put her hand out flat across the table towards Drewe, palm up.
'Pay—' she said, and stopped.

She did not finish the word. Her mouth stayed open on it. Her hand stayed out over the salt cellar, palm up, the fingers a little curled, and it did not move at all. Not a tremor. Her eyes did not blink. A crumb sat on her lower lip and stayed there.
I had read that a stalled person is a rigid, heavy body. I had not thought about what it would be like to sit across a table from one.
'She'll come back,' Tran said. 'Up to ten minutes.'
Drewe took two coppers out of her coat and laid them in Lisle's palm, one on top of the other. They sat there. The hand did not close.
The waiter came to sweep up the plate and looked at Lisle and then at me. I told him she was thinking. He went away.
She came back six minutes later by the clock over the counter.
'—up,' she said. Then she looked down at the two coppers in her hand. 'When did you pay?'
'Six minutes ago,' Drewe said. 'You took it very well.'

Lisle closed her hand on the coins. 'Robbed of six minutes' gloating,' she said. 'That's the third today. One this morning I was halfway up a ladder in the storeroom. Came down to the foreman writing my name in his book for standing about.'
She said it lightly. Her other hand, the one in her lap, had hold of her napkin and was twisting it.
'How many have you had?' I asked Drewe.
'Two,' she said. 'Small ones. I'm a light eater.'
'And you?' I said to Tran.
He opened his eyes a little further. 'None,' he said. 'Stiller. I owe sleep, not stalls.' He closed them again. 'Paying now.'

I saw Drewe's on the third morning, by chance, on my way across the street market to the Guild. She was at an ironmonger's stall with a paper of brass screws in one hand and a coin held out in the other. The ironmonger was waiting for the coin. It did not come.
She was quite still. The screws did not rattle in the paper. A boy with a basket walked into her shoulder and bounced off and looked back at her as if she had pushed him.
I stood beside her so that nobody else would walk into her. I did not try to move her. The ironmonger looked at me.
'She's thinking,' I said.
He served the woman behind her.
Four minutes later Drewe's hand finished putting the coin down on the board, and she looked round and saw me.
'Did I miss anything?'
'Four minutes.'
'Stalled at a stall,' she said. 'At least I picked the right sort.' She laughed at that herself, briefly, and then looked at her hand with the coin gone from it and did not laugh again.

That night at the night desk, between the hourly rounds, I took a sheet of graph paper from the stationery cupboard and ruled it into seven columns for the days and twenty-four rows for the hours. I gave each of them a band of colour. Lisle in red, Drewe in green, Tran in pencil.

Into Lisle's band I wrote what I knew. Ladder, storeroom, morning. Chophouse, evening, six minutes. Into Drewe's, the market and four minutes. Into Tran's I wrote 'asleep' wherever he had said he would be, which was most of it.

I did not know yet what it was for. I could not see any of them inside a Lull, and I never would. I could see them here, on paper, in the hours when they were not playing. That was all I had when I started.

The next evening I asked them for the rest. Drewe gave me her week down to the quarter hour: the shop, her family's bench, the tram, her bed. Tran gave me his in four words: 'Work. Sleep. Mm. Sleep.' Lisle said, 'Two coppers says you can't guess where I'll be on Friday at three.'
'I'm not guessing,' I said. 'I'm asking.'
She looked at me for a while, and then she told me.

The Night Audit filing had come to my desk on Cassius's second day in the post, with a note in his hand saying it would suit my thoroughness. I came in at four each afternoon to do it before the night desk opened at nine.

On the fourth afternoon the registry porter brought up a stack of maintenance orders bound in grey card. Each one was folded and sealed with the Senior Night Auditor's wafer. On each cover was a Guild order number, the words 'Public clock, maintenance', and a signature: C. Orme. There were forty of them, one clock each.

I knew what they were. These were the orders the Senior Night Auditor checks: that the work ordered was done, that the parts charged were the parts fitted, that the clock was signed off true. In March the committee had written to tell me that work would be mine.

By Guild rule a sealed order is opened by the post holder or on his written instruction. I had no instruction. I filed them in number order in the closed cabinet. Before I locked it I wrote the forty order numbers down the inside cover of my notebook, because I had been told to file them and nobody had told me not to read the covers. The dates and the clocks were inside the seals.
I did not know why I wanted the numbers. I wrote that down too.
On the fifth morning I went to Lisle's lodgings to collect her for the landing. She had not answered the note I sent about Saturday, and I wanted Saturday on the graph paper.

She opened the door in her coat with a slice of bread in her mouth. There was a letter on the mat between us. It had the Bank's grey seal. Under her name, on the cover, someone had written 'Re: Copper Stair paper'.
She took the bread out of her mouth and picked the letter up. She looked at the cover. She did not turn it over or put a finger under the flap. She dropped it into the coal bucket by the door.
'Copper Stair folded last year,' she said. 'They still write.'
'You played for them?'
'Two seasons.' She put the bread back in her mouth and pulled the door shut behind her.

I had watched her hands the whole time. They had not hesitated over the letter, not even for a second. My verdict was that she knew what was in it already. It was her letter and her business, and I did not ask. In the margin of her band on the graph paper, that night, I wrote 'Copper Stair' and nothing else.

On the landing that afternoon the plates were only floor. Without the Hour they were brass discs set in the boards, numbered I to XII, and the Arbor was a round platform with a rail that someone had hung a wet coat on.

Drewe sat on the edge of plate IX with her knees up. She had put the screwdriver away. In its place she was turning a small brass box over and over in her fingers: lid, base, lid, base. It was old and plain and worn smooth at the corners.
'What's that?' I asked.
'My gran's.' She turned it again. 'Snuffbox. She left me that and her opinions. The box was the smaller of the two.'
Lisle laughed. Tran did not open his eyes.
I watched Drewe's thumb. It went over the lid and round the hinge and over the base, and it never went to the catch. In the time I watched her she did not open it once.

My verdict was that it was a keepsake. She handled it the way people handle a dead relative's things: often, and without looking inside. I had seen people do it at the Guild with old winders' tools. I put it out of my mind.

The Bank's terms came on the fifth evening, to my desk at the Guild. The clerk from the porter's lodge brought them himself. He had the same ink on the same finger. He laid an envelope on my blotter, and beside it, a Bank pen.
There were two sheets inside. The first was a letter on the Bank's paper, signed for the Office of Issue with a signature I could not read.

'The Bank of Hours will confirm Miss P. Sandor as Reckoner of the Ninth Stair, and will issue her key and licence, on receipt of her signature to the enclosed report before midnight tonight. In the absence of her signature the Bank will refuse.'

The second sheet was the report. It was one paragraph. It said the scale in the porter's lodge of the Ninth Stair had been found on inspection to read forty-seven seconds high, and that the Ninth Stair's MD7 Close was in consequence correct as to Issue and Tally, and the result stood. There was a line at the bottom for my name.
I had checked that scale's empty pan myself. It had read nothing.

I knew the printed rules that applied, and I went through them in order because they were the only firm thing on the desk. The Bank must confirm or refuse an emergency Reckoner within seven days, and refusal is the Bank's call alone. Once it confirms, only the Arbiters' Court can take a licence away, for a proven offence, at an open hearing. The Bank cannot. The Sponsor's Right cannot be used for the same person twice. Whitlow's key works only for Whitlow. The Bank issues every key there is.
So this was the one day the Bank could still say no to me, and it had chosen to spend it on one word.
'Is there an answer, Miss Sandor?' the clerk asked.
'Not yet.'
He nodded, as if he had expected that, and left the pen where it was.
I was afraid. I looked at my own hands on the blotter, either side of the report, and watched them until they were still.

If I signed, I would put my name under a figure I knew was false, in my own hand, on the Bank's paper. If I did not, the Bank would refuse me. MD8 was the night after next, and without me the Ninth Stair had three players, and a side forfeits with fewer than four. They were twelfth of twelve.
The clock on my desk said six o'clock. I had six hours to sign a lie or never enter the Hour again.
